title: Ptolemy's chords on a circle of radius r
content: Ptolemy's Almagest tabulated chord lengths crd(α) = 2r·sin(α/2) of a circle of radius r as the foundation of ancient trigonometry. The parent gallery entry formalizes the chord engine on the unit circle to derive the sine addition formula. This file restores an explicit radius r and proves the two closed-form identities Ptolemy actually tabulated: the chord-length formula (distance between two points in terms of the central angle between them) and the law of cosines (third side of a triangle from two sides and the included angle). It then shows these agree on a single circle and that r=1 recovers the parent's lemma.

title: Cartesian form and the unit-circle squared chord
content: exp_ofReal_mul_I rewrites exp(θ·i) = cos θ + i·sin θ via Complex.exp_mul_I and the real/complex cos,sin coercions — this is what makes the real and imaginary parts literally cos θ and sin θ, keeping later algebra to a one-line linear_combination. normSq_one_sub_exp then computes ‖1 − exp(θ·i)‖² = (1−cos θ)² + sin²θ = 2 − 2cos θ. norm_exp_sub_exp factors out exp(b·i): since ‖exp(b·i)‖ = 1, ‖exp(a·i) − exp(b·i)‖ = ‖1 − exp((a−b)·i)‖, collapsing a two-point chord to a one-point chord.

title: The half-angle identity behind chord length
content: two_sub_two_cos proves 2 − 2cos t = (2 sin(t/2))², the squared-chord form of the half-angle identity cos t = 1 − 2 sin²(t/2). It follows from the double-angle formula cos(2x) = 2cos²x − 1 with x = t/2 and the Pythagorean identity. This single identity is what converts both the unit-chord computation and the law of cosines into the half-angle sine form Ptolemy used.

title: Chord-length formula on a radius-r circle
content: chord_length proves ‖r·e^{iθz} − r·e^{iθw}‖ = 2r·|sin((θz−θw)/2)| for r ≥ 0. The radius factors out of the difference, and since r ≥ 0 the norm of ↑r is r, reducing to the unit chord ‖1 − e^{i(θz−θw)}‖. That equals 2|sin((θz−θw)/2)| by squaring (normSq_one_sub_exp + two_sub_two_cos) and taking the nonnegative square root (nlinarith). This is exactly Ptolemy's crd(Δθ) = 2r·sin(Δθ/2) with the absolute value handling the unrestricted angle.

title: Law of cosines via the complex exponential
content: law_of_cosines proves ‖r₁·e^{iθ₁} − r₂·e^{iθ₂}‖² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂cos(θ₁−θ₂). Writing both exponentials in Cartesian form, the squared norm expands to (r₁cosθ₁ − r₂cosθ₂)² + (r₁sinθ₁ − r₂sinθ₂)²; grouping gives r₁²(cos²+sin²) + r₂²(cos²+sin²) − 2r₁r₂(cosθ₁cosθ₂ + sinθ₁sinθ₂), which is r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂cos(θ₁−θ₂) after cos_sub. The whole reduction is a single linear_combination over the two Pythagorean identities (coefficients r₁², r₂²). The cross term is exactly −2·Re(z·conj w), the inner product of the two position vectors.

title: Consistency on one circle, unit case, and a worked chord
content: law_of_cosines_eq_chord_sq and consistency show that on a single circle (r₁=r₂=r) the law of cosines value r²+r²−2r²cos Δθ equals the square of the chord length (2r·sin(Δθ/2))², the bridge being 1−cos t = 2sin²(t/2). chord_length_unit is the r=1 specialization recovering the parent's distance lemma. The worked example takes a radius-2 circle and central angle π/3 (a regular-hexagon edge): chord = 2·2·sin(π/6) = 4·(1/2) = 2, checked against chord_length and Real.sin_pi_div_six.
